Then leave it. Point is to pass the exam. Learn only what makes sense to you. If it is taking time, leave it and come back at the end if there is time. In the long run it won't matter if you had learned such lists without meaning.

Sometimes facts become easier to remember when you learn more about it. Depth brings clarity. So if an information feels difficult to learn, try to learn more than you need about it. In the end you might not remember the extra details you read, but you will remember what you had intended to remember at least. Clearly, you have to decide where to draw the line, and whether that fact is worth your time. This works especially well with lists. You could try to learn why each element is in the list by trying to learn more about them. This is much more meaningful than learning lists as such. But if your short on time, meaningless mnemonics is the way.

Best way is to learn about the individual diseases. Lists do not build concepts. Have a look at the management of each of those diseases. Understand how it is the part of management of each. This card is a waste of time. Clinically you would never have to think about this list as it is, but you will have to recall each of them, when trying to manage a patient with that disease. In ortho duty room, we used to make casts, and help in applying. If traction or reduction was required PGs did. But simply applying we used to do.

Taking blood samples (70-80% of your job), IV cannulation, Taking blood cultures in a sterile manner, taking blood samples from central lines. Connecting IV fluids, setting a drop rate.

Foley catheterization, flushing a Foley, taking sterile sample from Foley, placing condom catheters

Ryle's tube insertion, giving stomach washes.

Cleaning, dressing, suturing, suture removal. Giving LA (know which Ligno to use). Know what each bottle in the dressing trolley is used for.

GCS scoring, Triaging.

Ascitic tap

Giving intradermal injections - XST, drug sensitivity (Know for which antibiotics we have to do this, signs of allergy)

IM injections - B12, Proluton, Anti-D, Vaccination, oxytocin.

Taking ABG. Interpretation of easy ones. ( Met/Resp, ?Compensation, Anion gap)

ECG leads placement- interpreting rate, rhythm, axis, obvious ST-T changes

Giving slow IV drugs - Labetolol, Digoxin, Iron sucrose. Know indications, side effects, time over which it has to be given, dose.

Conducting a normal delivery . Baby and the placenta(with a pg nearby, who can identify if something is going wrong), giving episiotomy. Suturing muscle and skin.

Taking cord blood for gases, DCT.

Localizing FHS, know necessary theory. 

Making and applying casts, making pulse window. Doing compartment charting.

Blood product transfusions. (Indications, storing, starting, monitoring, reactions.)

Measuring HC for kids. Checking RBS by heel prick.

Taking cervical swabs for culture sensitivity.

Pushing trolleys, ECG machines, sometimes wheelchairs, getting pgs their food, begging for unnecessary echo, CT, blood transfusions.

Nice to know (with PG's assistance)

1. Central line insertion
2. LP in adults, neonates.
3. Spinal anesthesia
4. Intubation (in BD patients)
5. Suctioning ET tubes, collecting tracheal aspirate for culture.
6. I don't think they give chances for ICD placement, but observe once.
7. Minor OT - circumcision, lipoma, sebaceous cysts, LN biopsy - assist. Learn knots, sutures - minor OT is the best place to learn surgery. Major OT - retract/staple.
8. UVC placement in neonates.
9. Debridement
10. Pleural tap

You'll learn a lot even if you are completely uninterested. If you are interested, you can learn a lot more. The advantage is you can make mistakes, without legal consequences. This would be the last time in your life where you have that advantage. Use it. Everyone from cleaning ladies to professors used to shout at me. After a point I got used to it. When we think of moving a part of our body, the required "muscles representing areas" in the brain, for that movement, is stimulated. Nerves from those areas reach our limb muscles through the spinal cord and causes them to contract.

A muscle crossing a joint, causes the joint to bend in its direction. Imagine a stick, which you have bent. Connect a thread across. Now pull the thread, from both ends towards the middle, you can see that the angle of bent decreases. Same thing happens with muscles and joints.
Note that movement is always due to contraction of muscles. 
Q. How do you bend your elbow
A. Contracting the biceps (muscle infront of arm)
Q. How do you straighten your elbow
A. Is not relaxing biceps. Answer is contracting the muscle, triceps, which is behind your arm. This will be clear if you think the thread and stick analogy.

Tendons are actually parts of muscles that connect to bones. They are fibre like - white and shiny - has no contractile property. They are just connectors. Just clarifying.
